title: Exercise 15.3: Continuity and Discontinuity
notes: **Topic focus:** Checking continuity and identifying types of discontinuities.
**Three-condition test:** Verify all three conditions: f(a) defined, limit exists, limit equals f(a).
**Common problem types:** Piecewise functions, rational functions, absolute value functions.
**Identifying discontinuities:** Classify as removable, jump, or infinite based on limit behavior.
**Continuity on intervals:** A function is continuous on [a,b] if continuous at every point.
**Example type 1:** Check continuity of f(x) = (x²-1)/(x-1) at x = 1 (removable discontinuity).
**Example type 2:** Check continuity of piecewise function at boundary points.
**Example type 3:** Find values of constants that make a function continuous.
**Practice source:** Exercise 15.3 with continuity problems and detailed solutions.
confusion: Don't forget to check all THREE conditions — missing any one means discontinuity.
For piecewise functions, always check both LHL and RHL at boundary points separately.
Confusing continuity with differentiability — a function can be continuous but not differentiable.
Not checking if f(a) is defined before evaluating the limit.
Assuming rational functions are continuous everywhere without checking denominator zeros.
practice: Determine the values of k that make f(x) = {x²+k if x≤1, 2x+1 if x>1} continuous at x = 1.
Check continuity of f(x) = ⌊x⌋ (greatest integer function) at integer points.
Find all points of discontinuity of f(x) = 1/(x²-4) and classify them.
Show that f(x) = |x-2| is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at x = 2.
Determine k and m so that f(x) = {kx+1 if x≤2, mx²-1 if x>2} is continuous everywhere.
universalFacts: Continuity is preserved under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and composition of functions.
Polynomial functions are continuous everywhere — a fundamental result in analysis.
The intermediate value theorem requires continuity on a closed interval.
Continuous functions on closed intervals achieve maximum and minimum values (extreme value theorem).
Understanding continuity is essential for understanding derivatives and integrals.
